body.p: Index reviews and revisions After the index is finishedIndex reviews and revisions The indexer has finished the project and emailed it off to you. It is sitting in your mailbox, blinking balefully at you. You click on the paperclip and open it up. Now what do you do with it?

section.title: From Index to Text: Does the Index Serve New Readers?
section.p: Index evaluationfrom index to text Usersnew readers Start by thinking about someone new to the subject of the book. Pick a few topics that a prospective reader might look up. Can you find them easily in the index? Do the cross-references lead you to useful information? Are the subheadings helpful?

section.title: From Text to Index: Reviewing for Long-Term Value
section.p: Index evaluationfrom text to index Now work the other way: open the book at random, pick a significant discussion, and try to find it in the index. Can you access it from multiple entry points? Are the headings you would naturally look under present?

section.title: Errors
section.p: Index errors Spelling errors in indexes Error rate in indexes No index is perfect. Some errors are inevitable, especially in complex texts. The question is whether the error rate is acceptable. Common errors include misspellings, incorrect page numbers, inconsistent cross-references, and missing entries for important topics.

section.title: Revisions
section.p: Index reviews and revisionsprocess Communicationduring index revision process American Society of Indexers (ASI)H. W. Wilson Award When revisions are needed, communication is key. Group corrections by type, give specific examples, and ask questions rather than making accusations. The ASI’s H. W. Wilson Award for Excellence in Indexing demonstrates the high standards the profession aspires to.
